getDesignGroupSequential.label: O'Brien-Fleming-type alpha spending, 3 looks
getDesignGroupSequential.description: The most common group sequential design in practice: three analyses (two interim, one final) with an O'Brien-Fleming-type alpha spending function, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: Look at the efficacy boundaries on the z-value scale: the first interim boundary (about 3.71) is far stricter than the fixed-design 1.96, so an early stop needs overwhelming evidence. The final boundary (about 1.99) is barely above 1.96 - the price paid for two interim looks is small. Check the inflation factor: the maximum sample size grows by only about 2%. This is why O'Brien-Fleming-type designs dominate confirmatory practice. (Compare with typeOfDesign = "OF", the classic Wang-Tsiatis version: similar shape, boundaries 3.47 / 2.45 / 2.00.)

getDesignGroupSequential.label: Pocock-type alpha spending, 3 looks
getDesignGroupSequential.description: Same trial as the O'Brien-Fleming example but with a Pocock-type spending function, which spends alpha nearly evenly across looks. Run both and compare on the Summary and Plot tabs.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: The boundaries are nearly constant across stages (about 2.28 at every look), so stopping early is much easier than under O'Brien-Fleming - but the final boundary is well above 1.96, and the inflation factor is much larger. Pocock-type designs pay a real sample-size premium for aggressive early stopping, which is why they are less used for confirmatory trials.

getDesignGroupSequential.label: Adding a non-binding futility bound
getDesignGroupSequential.description: A two-stage O'Brien-Fleming-type design with a futility bound at the interim: if the z-value falls below 0 (the treatment looks no better than control), the trial may stop for futility. Non-binding means the efficacy boundaries remain valid even if the futility rule is ignored.
getDesignGroupSequential.interpretation: The summary now shows a futility boundary at the interim alongside the efficacy boundary. Because it is non-binding, the type I error is protected even if the sponsor continues despite crossing it; a binding futility bound would buy slightly lower efficacy boundaries in exchange for the obligation to stop. Note the 'futility probabilities' row: that is the chance of stopping for futility if the true effect is zero.

getDesignInverseNormal.label: Inverse normal combination, unequal information
getDesignInverseNormal.description: A three-stage adaptive design using the inverse normal combination test with O'Brien-Fleming-type spending and interim analyses at 40% and 70% of the information. The boundaries match the group sequential design - the difference is what the design permits later.
getDesignInverseNormal.interpretation: Compare this summary with getDesignGroupSequential using the same inputs: the boundaries are identical. The inverse normal design combines stage-wise p-values with fixed weights (derived from the planned information rates), which is what makes design adaptations - like a data-driven sample size increase at an interim - possible without inflating the type I error. That flexibility is invisible in the boundary table but is the whole point.

getDesignFisher.label: Fisher's combination test, 2 stages
getDesignFisher.description: A two-stage adaptive design based on Fisher's product of stage-wise p-values, with equal alpha for both stages and early stopping for futility if the first-stage p-value exceeds 0.5.
getDesignFisher.interpretation: Fisher's combination multiplies the stage-wise p-values and compares the product against a critical value. The summary shows the scale: critical values here live on the p-value product scale, not the z-scale. alpha0Vec = 0.5 means the trial stops for futility at stage 1 if p1 > 0.5. Fisher designs are fully adaptive but generally less efficient than inverse normal designs, so they appear mostly in small exploratory settings.

getDesignConditionalDunnett.label: Conditional Dunnett, interim at half the information
getDesignConditionalDunnett.description: A design for multi-arm trials with treatment selection: several treatment arms are compared with a shared control at an interim (at 50% of the information), promising arms continue, and the final analysis uses the conditional Dunnett test to protect the familywise error rate.
getDesignConditionalDunnett.interpretation: This design has no boundary table like the group sequential designs - the interim is for selecting arms, not for early efficacy claims. secondStageConditioning = TRUE conditions the final test on the first-stage data, which is more powerful than treating the stages independently. Use this design as input to the multi-arm analysis functions to see it in action.

getDesignCharacteristics.label: Characteristics of a saved design
getDesignCharacteristics.description: Computes the information and power characteristics of a design. It builds on the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design: create it in the Design tab and save it (the Learn path does this for you), then pick it in the design dropdown below.
getDesignCharacteristics.interpretation: The key numbers are the shift values: how much more information (roughly, sample size) the sequential design needs than a fixed design with the same alpha and power. For the O'Brien-Fleming example the inflation factor is about 1.02 - a 2% premium buys two chances to stop early. The average sample number (ASN) rows show the flip side: under the alternative, the expected sample size is well below the fixed-design requirement.

getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.label: Power curve for a saved design
getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.description: Computes overall power, stopping probabilities, and expected sample size of a saved design across a range of standardized effect sizes. It uses the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design from your saved work - create and save it in the Design tab if it isn't there yet.
getPowerAndAverageSampleNumber.interpretation: Read the table by column, one column per effect size theta. At theta = 0 the 'power' row shows the type I error (0.025); as theta grows, power rises and the average sample number (ASN) falls below nMax, because large effects make early stopping likely. This trade-off - a small maximum sample size premium for a much smaller expected sample size - is the core argument for group sequential designs. The Plot tab shows the same story as curves.

getGroupSequentialProbabilities.label: Exit probabilities for O'Brien-Fleming boundaries
getGroupSequentialProbabilities.description: The low-level engine behind the design functions: given a decision matrix of continuation regions (here the classic 3-look O'Brien-Fleming z-boundaries with no futility stopping) and the information rates, it computes the stage-wise boundary-crossing probabilities under the null hypothesis.
getGroupSequentialProbabilities.interpretation: Each column is a stage. The rows give the cumulative probabilities of falling below the lower row and above the upper row of the decision matrix under the null (drift 0). Check that the probabilities of crossing the upper boundaries sum (across stages, as increments) to alpha = 0.025 - that is exactly the constraint the design functions solve for when they compute boundaries. This function is worth one run just to demystify where the boundaries come from.

getFutilityBounds.label: Converting a futility bound between scales
getFutilityBounds.description: Futility rules are communicated on many scales - z-values, p-values, conditional power. This converts a futility bound of z = 0.5 to the one-sided p-value scale.
getFutilityBounds.interpretation: A z-value futility bound of 0.5 corresponds to a one-sided p-value of about 0.31: the trial would stop for futility when the interim result is weaker than p = 0.31. Being able to restate a rule on the scale your clinical team thinks in (often conditional power) is a routine communication task - try changing targetScale and see how the same rule reads on each scale.

getSampleSizeMeans.label: Continuous endpoint, fixed design
getSampleSizeMeans.description: The textbook calculation: a two-sample comparison of means with standardized effect 0.5 (difference 0.5, standard deviation 1), one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%, no interim analyses.
getSampleSizeMeans.interpretation: About 128 subjects in total (64 per group) - the classic answer for a medium standardized effect. Two things worth internalizing: sample size scales with (stDev/alternative)^2, so halving the effect quadruples the trial; and the efficacy boundary on the treatment-effect scale (0.35) tells you the smallest observed difference that would reach significance.

getSampleSizeMeans.label: Same trial with a group sequential design
getSampleSizeMeans.description: The identical means comparison, but run under the 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design from the Design tab. The design dropdown below picks it from your saved work (the Learn path saves it for you if you haven't).
getSampleSizeMeans.interpretation: Compare with the fixed-design example: the maximum sample size rises only from about 128 to 129 (the 2% inflation factor at work), but the expected sample size under the alternative drops to about 110, because the trial can stop at 43 or 86 subjects if the effect shows early. This pair of numbers - small maximum premium, large expected saving - is the entire sales pitch for group sequential designs.

getSampleSizeRates.label: Binary endpoint, 45% vs 30% response
getSampleSizeRates.description: A two-sample comparison of response rates: treatment is assumed to lift the response rate from 30% to 45%, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%, normal approximation.
getSampleSizeRates.interpretation: About 325 subjects in total for a 15-percentage-point improvement. Note how much larger this is than the continuous-endpoint example: binary endpoints carry less information per subject. Try moving pi2 to 0.5 while keeping the same 15-point difference - the required sample size grows, because variance pi(1-pi) is maximal near 0.5.

getSampleSizeSurvival.label: Survival endpoint, HR 0.7, median control survival 12 months
getSampleSizeSurvival.description: A time-to-event trial: control median survival 12 months, target hazard ratio 0.7, subjects accrued uniformly over 12 months with 12 months of additional follow-up, one-sided alpha 2.5%, power 80%.
getSampleSizeSurvival.interpretation: The driver of a survival trial is events, not subjects: about 247 events are needed for HR 0.7, and with this accrual and follow-up that translates into about 429 subjects and a 24-month trial. Play with followUpTime and watch the trade: longer follow-up means fewer subjects (each contributes more events) but a longer study - a budget-versus-calendar decision every survival trial faces.

getSampleSizeSurvival.label: Piecewise accrual and piecewise hazards
getSampleSizeSurvival.description: A more realistic setup: sites ramp up (15 subjects/month for the first year, 30/month for the second), and the control hazard is piecewise - 0.025/month in months 0-6, 0.04 in months 6-12, 0.015 thereafter. Target hazard ratio 0.7.
getSampleSizeSurvival.interpretation: The event requirement (about 247) is the same as in the simple example - it depends only on the hazard ratio, alpha, and power. What changes is everything else: 540 subjects accrue over 24 months, and because the late hazard is low (0.015/month), events arrive slowly - the required follow-up is about 25 months and the analysis lands near month 49. This is why realistic accrual and hazard assumptions matter: the statistics are the same, the calendar is not.

getSampleSizeCounts.label: Recurrent events, negative binomial
getSampleSizeCounts.description: A count-data endpoint (e.g. exacerbations per year): control rate 0.8 events per subject-year, target rate ratio 0.75, overdispersion 0.5, everyone observed for exactly one year.
getSampleSizeCounts.interpretation: About 744 subjects - count endpoints with overdispersion are expensive. Set overdispersion to 0 and rerun: the requirement drops sharply, because overdispersion (patient-to-patient heterogeneity beyond Poisson) dilutes the information each subject contributes. Under-guessing this parameter at the design stage is one of the classic ways recurrent-event trials end up underpowered.

getPowerMeans.label: Power curve under a saved sequential design
getPowerMeans.description: The flip side of sample size: fix the maximum sample size at 128 and ask what power the saved 3-look O'Brien-Fleming design achieves across a range of standardized effects. If it isn't in your saved work yet, create and save it in the Design tab first.
getPowerMeans.interpretation: Read the cumulative power row: 20% at effect 0.2, 61% at 0.4, 92% at 0.6, 99% at 0.8 - the S-shaped power curve every trialist carries in their head. Also read the expected-sample-size rows: at effect 0.8 the trial stops early so often that it averages just 85 subjects of the 128 maximum. The Plot tab draws both curves.

getPowerRates.label: Power for a range of response rates, n = 200
getPowerRates.description: With 200 subjects and a control response rate of 30%, how much power is there to detect treatment response rates from 40% to 60%?
getPowerRates.interpretation: Power climbs from 32% (pi1 = 0.40) through 59% (0.45) and 83% (0.50) to 99% (0.60). The sobering lesson: with n = 200, a real 10-point improvement is more likely missed than found. Power calculations before a trial protect you from exactly this - running a study that cannot answer its own question.

getPowerSurvival.label: Power for a range of hazard ratios, 200 events
getPowerSurvival.description: A survival trial with 400 subjects and 200 target events (control median 12 months, 12-month accrual): what is the power if the true hazard ratio is 0.6, 0.7, or 0.8?
getPowerSurvival.interpretation: Power is 95% at HR 0.6, 71% at 0.7, and only 35% at 0.8 - survival trials sized for optimistic hazard ratios are fragile against moderate effects. Note directionUpper = FALSE: benefit means a hazard ratio below 1, so power is directed towards smaller values; forgetting this flag computes power for the wrong tail (run it with TRUE and see the powers collapse).

getPowerCounts.label: Power for recurrent events, n = 400
getPowerCounts.description: With 400 subjects, control rate 0.8 events/year, and overdispersion 0.5: what is the power to detect rate ratios of 0.7 or 0.8? Benefit is a ratio below 1, hence directionUpper = FALSE.
getPowerCounts.interpretation: Power is about 71% for a rate ratio of 0.7 but only 37% for 0.8 - halving the effect (on the log scale) costs roughly half the power here. Together with the sample-size example (744 subjects for 80% power at ratio 0.75), this brackets the realistic operating range for the design.

getEventProbabilities.label: How fast do events accumulate?
getEventProbabilities.description: For a trial with 400 subjects accrued over 12 months, control hazard 0.05/month, and hazard ratio 0.8: what fraction of subjects will have had an event at months 6 through 30?
getEventProbabilities.interpretation: The cumulative event probability grows from 6% at month 6 to 23% at month 12 and 65% at month 30 - multiply by 400 to translate into expected event counts. This is the tool for answering the planning question survival designs live and die by: when will we reach the target number of events? Note the treatment arm (probabilities '1') lags the control arm - effective treatment slows down your own trial.

getNumberOfSubjects.label: Recruitment curve with a ramp-up
getNumberOfSubjects.description: Sites recruit 15 subjects/month for the first 6 months and 30/month for the next 6. How many subjects are on study at months 3 through 24?
getNumberOfSubjects.interpretation: The curve runs 45, 90, 180, 270 and then flattens - accrual ends at month 12 with 270 subjects (6 x 15 + 6 x 30). Piecewise accrual notation reads as intervals: c(0, 6, 12) with intensities c(15, 30) means 15/month on [0, 6) and 30/month on [6, 12]. Getting this notation right here makes the survival sample size functions, which use the same convention, much easier to read.

getAccrualTime.label: From relative site capacity to absolute intensities
getAccrualTime.description: Planned recruitment is known in relative terms - the second period runs at 1.5x the rate of the first (0.22 vs 0.33) over 30 months - and the trial needs 1000 subjects. What absolute rates does that imply?
getAccrualTime.interpretation: The relative intensities scale up to about 23.8 and 35.7 subjects/month so that the total reaches exactly 1000 by month 30. This mirrors how planning actually happens: feasibility teams provide relative ramp-up shapes, the statistician anchors them to the required sample size. The result can feed straight into getSampleSizeSurvival as the accrual specification.

getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.label: Piecewise hazards under a proportional effect
getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.description: The control hazard varies over time - 0.025/month in months 0-6, 0.04 in 6-12, 0.015 after - and treatment reduces it proportionally by 20% (hazard ratio 0.8). What are the treatment-arm hazards?
getPiecewiseSurvivalTime.interpretation: Each treatment hazard is exactly 0.8 x the control hazard (0.020, 0.032, 0.012) - that is what 'proportional hazards' means concretely: the ratio is constant even when the hazards themselves rise and fall. This object is the building block the survival sample size and simulation functions consume; inspect it here once and the piecewise notation elsewhere stops being mysterious.

getLambdaByMedian.label: Median survival to hazard rate
getLambdaByMedian.description: Clinicians quote median survival; the exponential model works in hazard rates. Convert a median of 12 months to its hazard rate.
getLambdaByMedian.interpretation: lambda = log(2) / median = 0.0578 events per subject-month. This one-line conversion is used constantly when translating clinical assumptions into design inputs - and it only holds under the exponential model, which is precisely the assumption worth questioning when survival curves plateau.

getHazardRatioByMedian.label: Medians to hazard ratio
getHazardRatioByMedian.description: Treatment is expected to extend median survival from 12 months (control) to 18 months. What hazard ratio does that correspond to under exponential survival?
getHazardRatioByMedian.interpretation: HR = median2 / median1 = 0.667 - a 50% longer median is the same statement as a one-third lower hazard. Clinical teams reason in medians, design functions want hazard ratios; this converter (and its inverses) is the bridge. It is exact only for exponential survival, a caveat that belongs in every protocol that uses it.

getPiByLambda.label: Hazard rate to event probability
getPiByLambda.description: With a hazard rate of 0.05 events per month, what is the probability a subject has an event within 12 months?
getPiByLambda.interpretation: pi = 1 - exp(-lambda x t) = 0.45: under this hazard, about 45% of subjects have an event within a year. This links the survival world (hazards) to the binary world (event proportions) - useful for sanity-checking hazard assumptions against published event rates, which are usually reported as proportions at a landmark time.
